narrative:
The model estimates a 66% probability that you will leave your job, meaning leaving is considered more likely than staying. That retention risk is why the promotion was denied: the decision is being driven by a forecast of possible departure, not by a claim that your work is unsatisfactory.

The strongest signal pushing toward “will leave” is that you have received other job opportunities. Among employees predicted to stay, only about one in four had such outside opportunities, so this pattern strongly raises the concern. The second most influential factor is your total experience of 11 or more years; only about 15% of employees predicted to stay have that level of experience, and in your profile it adds to the leave risk. Third is difficulty balancing work and personal life, which is much less common among employees predicted to stay—only around 9% report this difficulty—so it also pushes the prediction toward leaving.

What should happen next is a direct retention and career conversation rather than an automatic denial. The organization should explore why you are considering outside opportunities, whether the promotion timing can be clarified, and what flexible or workload changes would improve balance. You should also make your intentions and career expectations explicit, and raise any work-life balance concerns before deciding whether to pursue external options.
